title: Tyrus - TypeScript syntax Rust semantics
excerpt: A programming language made for devs
content_html:
Compiled backend language

Write familiar .tyr code

Tyrus uses concise syntax in .tyr files, then gives it native execution, deterministic memory semantics with NLL, precise diagnostics, and backend-focused tooling.

tyrus

const main = () => {
    print("Hello, World!");
};

Language superpowers

Validator decorations

Built-in rules like @email, @minLength, and @min, plus custom rules declared with validator function. Declarative validation with zero boilerplate.

Compile-time comptime

Execute pure logic at compilation time with comptime(...). Precompute lookup tables, math constants, and configurations with zero runtime overhead.

Sealed env and mirror

Encrypt .env into target/<profile>/.env.sealed with binary fingerprints. The .env.example mirror automatically stays in sync on every change.

Types

Integers and floats u8..u128, i8..i128, f32..f128, decimal, boolean, string, char, and first-class Result<T, E> types.

Deterministic memory safety

Ownership, borrowing, and NLL.

Memory safety without a garbage collector. Non-Copy types move on assignment, while borrows are verified at compile time. With Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL), borrows expire after their last actual use, freeing variables for immediate mutation without waiting for scope exit.

tyrus

const greeting: string = "hello";
const copy: string = greeting;

print(copy); // hello
print(greeting); // error: `greeting` was moved to `copy`

Scope-based cleanup

Run cleanup always, or only on errors.

defer runs when the scope exits. errdefer runs only when a Result or optional return exits with an error, making rollback paths explicit.

Learn about deferred cleanup

tyrus

function transfer(ok: boolean): Result<void, string> {
    defer print("cleanup"); // cleanup
    errdefer print("rollback"); // rollback

    if (!ok) {
        return Err("transfer failed");
    }
    
    return Ok();
}

const main = (): void => {
    match (transfer(false)) {
        Ok() => print("transfer complete"); // transfer complete
        Err(error) => printError(error); // transfer failed
    }
};

Exhaustive pattern matching

Match any shape. Narrow every branch.

Tagged unions, algebraic enum variants, and match with guard clauses give you exhaustive control flow. The compiler ensures every variant is handled and narrows types inside each arm.

tyrus

const main = () => {
    const getLetterGrade = (score: u8): string => {
        match (score) {
            90..=100 => "A";
            80..=89 => "B";
            70..=79 => "C";
            60..=69 => "D";
            0..=59 => "F";
            _ => "Invalid Score";
        }
    };

    print(getLetterGrade(95)); // A
};

No null. No undefined. Just T?

Absence is a state, not a value.

A bare return; produces absence. ?. and ?? propagate it safely. The compiler forces you to handle the absent case before the value reaches production, no runtime surprises.

tyrus

const findAccount = (id: i32): Account? => {
    if (id > 0) {
        return { id, nickname: "ada" };
    }
    
    return;  // absence
};

const account: Account? = findAccount(1);
print(account?.nickname ?? "anon");

// Uninitialized optional starts empty
let pending: i32?;
print(pending ?? 0);  // 0

Explicit success and failure

Represent recoverable errors with Result.

Result<T, E> carries either an Ok value or an Err value. Match both variants or propagate an error with ?.

Learn about Result

tyrus

function lookupName(found: boolean): Result<string, string> {
    if (found) {
        return Ok("Ada");
    }
    
    return Err("user not found");
}

const main = (): void => {
    match (lookupName(false)) {
        Ok(name) => print(name);
        Err(message) => printError(message); // user not found
    }
};

Handle errors at the call site

Keep the success path clear with onfail.

Attach an error handler to a Result initializer. The handler sees the error, while the binding holds the success value when execution continues.

Learn about onfail

tyrus

function lookupName(found: boolean): Result<string, string> {
    if (found) {
        return Ok("Ada");
    }

    return Err("user not found");
}

function showName(found: boolean): void {
    const name = lookupName(found) onfail {
        printError(name); // user not found

        return;
    };
    
    print(name); // Ada
}

const main = () => showName(true);

Pipe operator

Data flows top to bottom.

The |> operator threads values through function chains. The % topic token lets you place the piped value exactly where it belongs, no intermediate variables, no nesting.

tyrus

const main = (): void => {
    const double = (n: i64): i64 => n * 2;
    const increment = (n: i64): i64 => n + 1;
    const clamp = (value: i64, min: i64, max: i64): i64 => value < min ? min : value > max ? max : value;

    // Pipe chains read top-to-bottom
    const result: i64 = 5
        |> double
        |> increment
        |> double;  // 5 -> 10 -> 11 -> 22

    // Topic token % places the piped value exactly
    const clamped: i64 = 80 |> clamp(30, %, 100); // 80
    print(clamped); // 80
};

Native asynchronous code

Write async functions and await their results.

async functions return Promise<T>. Use await to read the value when the asynchronous operation completes.

Learn about async and await

tyrus

async function loadName(): Promise<string> {
    return "Ada";
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
    const name = await loadName();
    
    print(`Hello, ${name}`); // Hello, Ada
}

High-performance numeric kernels

Algebraic floating-point methods.

Primitives f32 and f64 provide algebraicAdd, algebraicSub, algebraicMul, algebraicDiv, and algebraicRem. They explicitly grant the compiler permission to reassociate floating-point calculations for SIMD vectorization and hardware-accelerated math kernels.

tyrus

const main = (): void => {
    const left: f64 = 6.0;
    const right: f64 = 4.0;

    // Explicit compiler permission for fast-math reassociation:
    const sum: f64 = left.algebraicAdd(right);
    const diff: f64 = left.algebraicSub(right);
    const prod: f64 = left.algebraicMul(right);
    const quot: f64 = left.algebraicDiv(right);
    const rem: f64 = left.algebraicRem(right);

    print(prod); // 24.0
};

Production secret protection

Sealed env and auto-synced .env.example.

Setting security.envSealed encrypts .env into target/<profile>/.env.sealed with asymmetric keys and embeds a binary fingerprint so containers never deploy plaintext secrets. In development, the compiler automatically mirrors keys and comments into .env.example with values cleared.

json

{
  "security": {
    "envFile": ".env",
    "envSealed": true
  }
}

text

# .env (local secrets)         # .env.example (mirrored & committed)
@type(u16)                     @type(u16)
@port()                        @port()
PORT=8080                      PORT=

@type(string)                  @type(string)
@startsWith("postgres://")     @startsWith("postgres://")
DATABASE_URL=postgres://...    DATABASE_URL=

@type(string)                  @type(string)
@minLength(16)                 @minLength(16)
API_SECRET=super_secret_value  API_SECRET=

Typed ORM and ODM

Use one Model API with SQL and MongoDB.

Define models as typed interfaces and query them asynchronously. The same Model API supports relational databases and MongoDB, with recoverable failures returned as Result.

Explore the database module

tyrus

import { User } from "./models/User";

async function main(): Promise<void> {
    const users = await User.findMany({ active: true });
}

Compile-time evaluation

Run code during compilation. Zero runtime cost.

Functions declared with comptime execute during compilation and embed their result as static scalars or literals directly into the binary. Calculate lookup tables, mathematical constants, and configurations with complete type safety.

tyrus

comptime function fibonacci(index: i32): i64 {
    let previous: i64 = 0;
    let current: i64 = 1;

    for (let pos: i32 = 0; pos < index; pos++) {
        const next: i64 = previous + current;
        previous = current;
        current = next;
    }

    return previous;
}

// Evaluated once at compile time, zero runtime calculation:
const maxLimit: i64 = comptime(fibonacci(50));

const main = (): void => {
    print(maxLimit); // 12586269025
};

Interactive exploration

Try in the terminal. Run in the browser.

Explore Tyrus instantly without project setup. tyrus repl provides an interactive console with in-process LLVM JIT evaluation, multi-line editing, session save/restore, and :type inspection. Or open the Web Playground at playground.tyruslang.org to write, compile to WebAssembly, and run code directly in your browser with shareable links.

text

tyrus repl
  ______                         ____  __________  __ 
 /_  __/_  _________  _______   / __ \/ ____/ __ \/ / 
  / / / / / / ___/ / / / ___/  / /_/ / __/ / /_/ / /  
 / / / /_/ / /  / /_/ (__  )  / _, _/ /___/ ____/ /___
/_/  \__, /_/   \__,_/____/  /_/ |_/_____/_/   /_____/
    /____/                                            

Type :help for available commands.

tyrus> :help
Commands (prefix with :):
  :help                              Show this help
  :clear                             Clear screen and session buffer
  :load <file>                       Load and evaluate a .tyr file
  :type <expr>                       Show the inferred type of an expression
  :doc <symbol>                      Show documentation for a symbol
  :edit                              Edit session buffer in external editor ($EDITOR)
  :save <name.tyr>                   Save session buffer to ~/.tyrus/repl/<name>.tyr
  :restore <name|file> [--merge|-m]  Restore a saved session (resets first; --merge keeps the current buffer)
  :delete <name>                     Delete a saved session from ~/.tyrus/repl
  :list                              List sessions saved via :save (~/.tyrus/repl)
  :reset                             Reset the entire session
  :exit                              Exit the REPL
  :quit                              Alias for :exit
  :q                                 Alias for :exit

Multi-line input is auto-detected by bracket matching.
tyrus>

A language toolchain, not just a parser

Interactive REPL & CLI

tyrus repl for in-process LLVM JIT evaluation, tyrus dev for live reload, and tyrus fmt for zero-config formatting.

Diagnostics & tyrus explain

Stable error codes with tyrus explain, accurate ranges, help messages, runtime failure examples, and editor Quick Fixes.

Editors powered by LSP

Completion, hover, signature help, inlay hints, semantic tokens, and code actions for VS Code, Neovim, Zed, IntelliJ, and Kate.

Web Playground & tests

Run in the browser via WebAssembly at playground.tyruslang.org, and run local test suites with tyrus test for *.test.tyr files.

Source formatting

Tyrus Formatter

tyrus fmt formats `.tyr` files consistently and applies the options in the project's tyrus-fmt.json.

Read the Formatter guide

tyrus-fmt.json

json

{
  "indent_style": "spaces",
  "indent_width": 4,
  "line_width": 90,
  "quote_style": "double"
}

Code analysis

Tyrus Lint

tyrus lint reports style, correctness, safety, performance, and architecture issues. Set each rule's severity in the project's tyrus-lint.json.

Read the Lint guide

tyrus-lint.json

json

{
  "no-unused-vars": "warn",
  "no-unused-imports": "warn",
  "prefer-const": "warn",
  "no-force-unwrap": "error"
}

Batteries included

Built-in native modules.

Everything required to build resilient backend services, CLI tools, and systems software is built into the Tyrus runtime.

tyrus:algorithmOver 50 built-in algorithms and data structures: Dijkstra, A*, Trie, and Red-Black Tree.tyrus:archiveTar and Zip archive creation, inspection, and extraction.tyrus:cliInteractive terminal prompts: select, multiselect, password, confirm, and input.tyrus:compressZstandard, Brotli, Gzip, and Deflate compression and decompression streams.tyrus:cryptoArgon2, SHA-256, SHA-512, AES-GCM, HMAC, JWT, UUID v7, and CSPRNG.tyrus:dbIntegrated database client and ORM for PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and MongoDB.tyrus:encodingHex, Base64, URL encoding, Varint, CSV, and JSON native codecs.tyrus:fsAsync and sync filesystem, atomic writes, streaming, glob, and file watching.tyrus:httpHTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 server, automatic routes, Swagger, and WebSocket.tyrus:mathConstants, trigonometry, number theory, geometry, and combinatorics.tyrus:memoryDeterministic memory operations: sizeOf, alignOf, zeroize, swap, and replace.tyrus:netTCP and UDP sockets, DNS resolution, reverse lookup, ping, and traceroute.tyrus:osSystem metadata, CPU cores, memory stats, temperatures, and native notifications.tyrus:processChild processes, command execution, signals, and resource monitoring.tyrus:simdPortable vector math intrinsics for high-throughput numeric operations.tyrus:streamComposable binary and text streaming primitives for high-performance I/O.tyrus:taskAsync runtime, multi-thread spawn, channels, mutex, rwlock, and cancellation.tyrus:temporalModern date, time, duration, and timezone handling with ergonomic syntax.tyrus:testBuilt-in test runner with describe, it, and expect for *.test.tyr files.tyrus:utilsTerminal text styling with styleText, ANSI colors, and ASCII FIGlet banners.

Safety feedback while you type

Errors are part of the product experience.

Compiler and linter diagnostics flow through the same analysis pipeline used by the CLI and the Language Server, so the terminal and editor agree on what is wrong and how to fix it.

error

tyrus

const maxUsers: u32 = "100"; 
let retries: u32 = 3;

print(retries);

text

error[E0308]: type mismatch for `maxUsers`: expected `u32`, found `string`
at /src/main.tyr:1:7
const maxUsers: u32 = "100";
      ^^^^^^^^
help: change the value or the annotation so their types match; convert numbers explicitly with `value as <type>`

Start with one command

shell

tyrus new

Run with one command

shell

tyrus run

Why the name

A rock and a god.

Tyrus is the Latin spelling of Tyre, the Phoenician city whose name means "rock". Tyr is the Norse god of war, justice, and courage.

But the name is a combination of the initials of TypeScript and Rust.

content_html_zh:
Compiled backend language

Write familiar .tyr code

Tyrus uses concise syntax in .tyr files, then gives it native execution, deterministic memory semantics with NLL, precise diagnostics, and backend-focused tooling.

tyrus

const main = () => {
    print("Hello, World!");
};

Language superpowers

Validator decorations

Built-in rules like @email, @minLength, and @min, plus custom rules declared with validator function. Declarative validation with zero boilerplate.

Compile-time comptime

Execute pure logic at compilation time with comptime(...). Precompute lookup tables, math constants, and configurations with zero runtime overhead.

Sealed env and mirror

Encrypt .env into target/<profile>/.env.sealed with binary fingerprints. The .env.example mirror automatically stays in sync on every change.

Types

Integers and floats u8..u128, i8..i128, f32..f128, decimal, boolean, string, char, and first-class Result<T, E> types.

Deterministic memory safety

Ownership, borrowing, and NLL.

Memory safety without a garbage collector. Non-Copy types move on assignment, while borrows are verified at compile time. With Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL), borrows expire after their last actual use, freeing variables for immediate mutation without waiting for scope exit.

tyrus

const greeting: string = "hello";
const copy: string = greeting;

print(copy); // hello
print(greeting); // error: `greeting` was moved to `copy`

Scope-based cleanup

Run cleanup always, or only on errors.

defer runs when the scope exits. errdefer runs only when a Result or optional return exits with an error, making rollback paths explicit.

Learn about deferred cleanup

tyrus

function transfer(ok: boolean): Result<void, string> {
    defer print("cleanup"); // cleanup
    errdefer print("rollback"); // rollback

    if (!ok) {
        return Err("transfer failed");
    }
    
    return Ok();
}

const main = (): void => {
    match (transfer(false)) {
        Ok() => print("transfer complete"); // transfer complete
        Err(error) => printError(error); // transfer failed
    }
};

Exhaustive pattern matching

Match any shape. Narrow every branch.

Tagged unions, algebraic enum variants, and match with guard clauses give you exhaustive control flow. The compiler ensures every variant is handled and narrows types inside each arm.

tyrus

const main = () => {
    const getLetterGrade = (score: u8): string => {
        match (score) {
            90..=100 => "A";
            80..=89 => "B";
            70..=79 => "C";
            60..=69 => "D";
            0..=59 => "F";
            _ => "Invalid Score";
        }
    };

    print(getLetterGrade(95)); // A
};

No null. No undefined. Just T?

Absence is a state, not a value.

A bare return; produces absence. ?. and ?? propagate it safely. The compiler forces you to handle the absent case before the value reaches production, no runtime surprises.

tyrus

const findAccount = (id: i32): Account? => {
    if (id > 0) {
        return { id, nickname: "ada" };
    }
    
    return;  // absence
};

const account: Account? = findAccount(1);
print(account?.nickname ?? "anon");

// Uninitialized optional starts empty
let pending: i32?;
print(pending ?? 0);  // 0

Explicit success and failure

Represent recoverable errors with Result.

Result<T, E> carries either an Ok value or an Err value. Match both variants or propagate an error with ?.

Learn about Result

tyrus

function lookupName(found: boolean): Result<string, string> {
    if (found) {
        return Ok("Ada");
    }
    
    return Err("user not found");
}

const main = (): void => {
    match (lookupName(false)) {
        Ok(name) => print(name);
        Err(message) => printError(message); // user not found
    }
};

Handle errors at the call site

Keep the success path clear with onfail.

Attach an error handler to a Result initializer. The handler sees the error, while the binding holds the success value when execution continues.

Learn about onfail

tyrus

function lookupName(found: boolean): Result<string, string> {
    if (found) {
        return Ok("Ada");
    }

    return Err("user not found");
}

function showName(found: boolean): void {
    const name = lookupName(found) onfail {
        printError(name); // user not found

        return;
    };
    
    print(name); // Ada
}

const main = () => showName(true);

Pipe operator

Data flows top to bottom.

The |> operator threads values through function chains. The % topic token lets you place the piped value exactly where it belongs, no intermediate variables, no nesting.

tyrus

const main = (): void => {
    const double = (n: i64): i64 => n * 2;
    const increment = (n: i64): i64 => n + 1;
    const clamp = (value: i64, min: i64, max: i64): i64 => value < min ? min : value > max ? max : value;

    // Pipe chains read top-to-bottom
    const result: i64 = 5
        |> double
        |> increment
        |> double;  // 5 -> 10 -> 11 -> 22

    // Topic token % places the piped value exactly
    const clamped: i64 = 80 |> clamp(30, %, 100); // 80
    print(clamped); // 80
};

Native asynchronous code

Write async functions and await their results.

async functions return Promise<T>. Use await to read the value when the asynchronous operation completes.

Learn about async and await

tyrus

async function loadName(): Promise<string> {
    return "Ada";
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
    const name = await loadName();
    
    print(`Hello, ${name}`); // Hello, Ada
}

High-performance numeric kernels

Algebraic floating-point methods.

Primitives f32 and f64 provide algebraicAdd, algebraicSub, algebraicMul, algebraicDiv, and algebraicRem. They explicitly grant the compiler permission to reassociate floating-point calculations for SIMD vectorization and hardware-accelerated math kernels.

tyrus

const main = (): void => {
    const left: f64 = 6.0;
    const right: f64 = 4.0;

    // Explicit compiler permission for fast-math reassociation:
    const sum: f64 = left.algebraicAdd(right);
    const diff: f64 = left.algebraicSub(right);
    const prod: f64 = left.algebraicMul(right);
    const quot: f64 = left.algebraicDiv(right);
    const rem: f64 = left.algebraicRem(right);

    print(prod); // 24.0
};

Production secret protection

Sealed env and auto-synced .env.example.

Setting security.envSealed encrypts .env into target/<profile>/.env.sealed with asymmetric keys and embeds a binary fingerprint so containers never deploy plaintext secrets. In development, the compiler automatically mirrors keys and comments into .env.example with values cleared.

json

{
  "security": {
    "envFile": ".env",
    "envSealed": true
  }
}

text

# .env (local secrets)         # .env.example (mirrored & committed)
@type(u16)                     @type(u16)
@port()                        @port()
PORT=8080                      PORT=

@type(string)                  @type(string)
@startsWith("postgres://")     @startsWith("postgres://")
DATABASE_URL=postgres://...    DATABASE_URL=

@type(string)                  @type(string)
@minLength(16)                 @minLength(16)
API_SECRET=super_secret_value  API_SECRET=

Typed ORM and ODM

Use one Model API with SQL and MongoDB.

Define models as typed interfaces and query them asynchronously. The same Model API supports relational databases and MongoDB, with recoverable failures returned as Result.

Explore the database module

tyrus

import { User } from "./models/User";

async function main(): Promise<void> {
    const users = await User.findMany({ active: true });
}

Compile-time evaluation

Run code during compilation. Zero runtime cost.

Functions declared with comptime execute during compilation and embed their result as static scalars or literals directly into the binary. Calculate lookup tables, mathematical constants, and configurations with complete type safety.

tyrus

comptime function fibonacci(index: i32): i64 {
    let previous: i64 = 0;
    let current: i64 = 1;

    for (let pos: i32 = 0; pos < index; pos++) {
        const next: i64 = previous + current;
        previous = current;
        current = next;
    }

    return previous;
}

// Evaluated once at compile time, zero runtime calculation:
const maxLimit: i64 = comptime(fibonacci(50));

const main = (): void => {
    print(maxLimit); // 12586269025
};

Or open the Web Playground at playground.tyruslang.org to write, compile to WebAssembly, and run code directly in your browser with shareable links.

A language toolchain, not just a parser

Interactive REPL & CLI

tyrus repl for in-process LLVM JIT evaluation, tyrus dev for live reload, and tyrus fmt for zero-config formatting.

Diagnostics & tyrus explain

Stable error codes with tyrus explain, accurate ranges, help messages, runtime failure examples, and editor Quick Fixes.

Editors powered by LSP

Completion, hover, signature help, inlay hints, semantic tokens, and code actions for VS Code, Neovim, Zed, IntelliJ, and Kate.

Web Playground & tests

Run in the browser via WebAssembly at playground.tyruslang.org, and run local test suites with tyrus test for *.test.tyr files.

  "indent_style": "spaces",

  "no-unused-vars": "warn",

  "no-force-unwrap": "error"

Safety feedback while you type

Errors are part of the product experience.

Compiler and linter diagnostics flow through the same analysis pipeline used by the CLI and the Language Server, so the terminal and editor agree on what is wrong and how to fix it.

error

tyrus

const maxUsers: u32 = "100"; 
let retries: u32 = 3;

print(retries);

text

error[E0308]: type mismatch for `maxUsers`: expected `u32`, found `string`
at /src/main.tyr:1:7
const maxUsers: u32 = "100";
      ^^^^^^^^
help: change the value or the annotation so their types match; convert numbers explicitly with `value as <type>`

Start with one command

shell

tyrus new

Run with one command

shell

tyrus run

为什么叫这个名字

A rock and a god.

Tyrus is the Latin spelling of Tyre, the Phoenician city whose name means "rock". Tyr is the Norse god of war, justice, and courage.

But the name is a combination of the initials of TypeScript and Rust.
